frontier.hypothesis: F31 (NEW, and now the top item) - because the residual block is measured fork-SENSITIVE, the C search must be re-run with cc1psx as the calibration ORACLE rather than the open-port cc1: score candidate spellings by how close cc1psx's emission is to target, since cc1psx is the compiler that actually built the target and is already strictly closer than the open port on two counts.
frontier.mechanism: tools/cc1psx_wrapper.sh runs PsyQ cc1psx.exe (2.7.2.SN.1) as a drop-in cc1 on preprocessed C at ~0.8s/invocation, sanctioned for calibration/self-disproof (never a build path). The sandbox score is computed against the open-port build, so it is the WRONG gradient for a fork-sensitive construct; a cc1psx-scored gradient is a different and better-aligned objective. If some spelling makes cc1psx emit target's block exactly, that spelling is the original source shape, and the remaining question becomes the separate, tractable one of what the open port does with THAT spelling.
frontier.next_probe: Reuse tmp/grind/CD_datasync/s18/psx.sh (preprocess -> open.s + psx.s) and cmp.py (block extraction + alignment against asm/funcs/CD_datasync.s) to build a small sweep driver that scores a body variant by cc1psx block distance. Start with the 14 forms banked this session plus the four rigid attractors, since their open-port scores are already known and the cc1psx scores are the new information. Report the cc1psx-vs-open-port score correlation - if it is weak, that alone explains 18 sessions of a flat open-port floor.

frontier.next_probe: Write schedsim.py replaying the backward pass over the decoded DAG; VALIDATE against all four banked chassis traces first; then enumerate C-emittable pre-sched orders (statement boundaries x value/address x inline, which is a small finite set given this session's measurements) and report which replay to target. A universal negative is proof-grade for the whole argument-block axis on the open port - and, crucially, should then be re-run against cc1psx's scheduler per F31, since the fork is now known to matter.

frontier.hypothesis: F30 (carried) - the identical block should be attacked on the sibling CD_sync (splat cpu_side_move_dir_4), which shares target's block order but differs in register pressure and in arg3's spelling, so a mechanism that is really about the block must behave identically on both.
frontier.mechanism: Same 14-insn target sequence, same early-lw-a3 failure, different chassis: the sibling names BOTH arg4 and arg5, has no do{}while(0) wrapper, and spells arg3 as the inline global D_800A11DC[D_800A11D5] rather than a hoisted-base load. Anything that behaves differently there is chassis pressure, and that difference is itself a measurement.
frontier.next_probe: Point tmp/grind/saEft01Init/s16/blockdump.py at the sibling's function section in the same banked dump and compare its sched1 pick trace with the one decoded this session, specifically whether its decisive pick pair is the same LUID race.
